sources.entry: Attabench - Attabench is a microbenchmarking app for macOS, designed to measure and visualize the performance of Swift code.

summary.one_liner: Attabench is a macOS microbenchmarking app that measures and charts the performance of Swift code, now largely superseded by the Swift Collections Benchmark package.
summary.what_it_does: Attabench runs repeated timings of low-level operations over input sizes and plots the results live on log-log charts. Users open a .attabench benchmark document (a folder with a run.sh script) and a .attaresult document stores timings so runs can be stopped and resumed. The task list can be filtered with a search field that supports negation, AND and OR expressions, and the run options control iterations, min and max duration. The right-hand panel changes chart appearance, including themes, scale types, curve data (minimum, average, maximum, sample count) and error bands based on standard deviation. Charts can be exported as PNG by dragging, and an attachart command-line target renders charts in batch. Benchmarks are written in Swift as a Swift package, and the README describes a JSON-based IPC protocol for benchmarks written in other languages.
use_cases: measure performance of Swift collection algorithms
plot algorithm runtime against input size on log-log charts
compare timings of several Swift implementations
generate chart images of benchmark results
investigate cache effects in lookup or search code
how_to_run: Build and run the Attabench target in Xcode 9, then press ⌘-R to start benchmarking
notable: Live-updating log-log charts while benchmarks run
Benchmark documents restartable via .attaresult results files
Error bands based on min, max and mean plus or minus sigma multiples
Language-agnostic IPC protocol using a named FIFO and JSON messages
Command-line attachart tool for batch chart rendering
caveats: The README warns that the package has been largely superseded by the Swift Collections Benchmark package.
Targets macOS only and requires Xcode 9 and Carthage to build, according to the README.
The author describes the code as messy and made for a single use case; themes can only be changed by editing the source.
